stories.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO days after board ruled out his return
stories.dek: President Trump says he 'made the deal' with the board; Nvidia's shares jumped about 32% on Monday, and lawmakers from both parties are questioning the decision.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive less than two weeks after he resigned, following contact from the White House. Shares rose about 32%, adding more than $1tn in market value, while lawmakers in both parties called for scrutiny.
body: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned, following direct contact from President Donald Trump, who told CNBC: "I made the deal."

Nvidia shares rose 32% in New York, adding more than $1tn to the company's market value, according to The Guardian. The Wall Street Journal put the gain at nearly $1 trillion. The Nasdaq composite rose 6.5% and the S&P 500 rose 4.7%.

Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is suspected by US authorities of spying for China, and with Nvidia employees. Beijing denies the spying allegation. Nvidia named finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO.

CNBC, citing three people familiar with the board's thinking, reported that senior administration officials contacted the board overnight on Friday to say Huang had not violated national security laws. The board then spoke with Huang over the weekend. A personal promise from Trump on Sunday sealed the decision, the sources said.

Trump said the board had asked for guarantees that Huang was not a national security threat. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," he said. He said Attorney General Todd Blanche's department felt Huang was "exonerated". Asked whether Huang would have returned without him, Trump said: "The answer is no."

On November 17, board chair Harvey Jones had told analysts the board did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO". Nvidia's shares had fallen by about a quarter after the resignation, and some investors and employees questioned Kress's leadership, CNBC reported.

In a statement, Nvidia said the board was "satisfied with respect to Mr Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia" and was confident his return "poses no national security risk". An independent investigation into allegations that Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation will continue, the company said.

The Commerce Department added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist on Monday. The Justice and Commerce departments said on November 17 they were investigating the firm over possible diversion of Nvidia chips to China.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton vowed that Congress would investigate. Representative Don Bacon criticised the administration's "inexplicable desire to save Huang". Senator Elizabeth Warren called the reinstatement "reckless". Senator Ruben Gallego called Trump's role "as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen".
Huang is due for a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1. Fox News reported he will appear before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
keyFacts: Huang resigned on November 12 and was reinstated on Monday, November 23.
Nvidia shares rose 32% on Monday, adding more than $1tn in value, per The Guardian.
Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist on Monday.
Huang faces closed-door House interviews on December 1 and a Senate Banking hearing on December 3.
stories.background:
Nvidia is the dominant supplier of AI processors, and its share price fell sharply after Huang's exit, alongside a wider AI sell-off. US agencies are investigating Megaspeed over suspected diversion of advanced chips to China in breach of export controls. California is also investigating.

BBC reported that Trump has bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m since returning to the White House. The White House has rejected claims that he profits from the presidency.
stories.whyItMatters: Nvidia's stock affects wider markets, and Congress is examining whether advanced chips reached China in breach of US export controls.

stories.headline: Modi announces ₹15,000-crore package for Nepal during PM Balen Shah's first Delhi visit
stories.dek: The leaders signed eight MoUs, agreed to an IIT campus in Nepal and flagged off an Ayodhya–Janakpur train, while leaving the boundary dispute to officials.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a ₹15,000-crore development package for Nepal after talks with Prime Minister Balendra Shah in New Delhi on Monday. The two sides also released a joint vision document and flagged off a rail service between Ayodhya and Janakpur.
body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a development package worth ₹15,000 crore for Nepal on Monday after talks in New Delhi with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, known as Balen Shah, on his first visit to India as prime minister.

The package is equivalent to NPR 24,000 crore, or about $1.6 billion. It includes ₹3,500 crore in grants for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure, and a rupee-denominated line of credit of ₹11,500 crore for energy projects. Firstpost reported that specific projects and modalities will be settled through mutual consultations.

The two leaders signed eight MoUs and, mostly by video link, laid foundation stones and inaugurated cross-border projects. They flagged off the Sarayu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya and Janakpur, inaugurated a road bridge linking Dharchula in Uttarakhand with Darchula in Nepal, and laid the foundation stone for an Integrated Check Post at Banbasa.

On energy, they dedicated Phase II of the Motihari–Amlekhgunj petroleum pipeline to Nepal and laid the foundation stone for a petroleum terminal at Jhapa and for the 669-MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project. Modi also said Nepal would get access to India's Kandla port, with Paradip port to follow once the necessary infrastructure is in place.
India will set up an offshore IIT campus in Nepal, Modi said. He also announced start-up incubators, an innovation hub and more scholarships in law and technology for Nepali students in India.

A 10-point joint vision document, titled Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal, calls for an updated legal framework, including a review of the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship on the basis of mutual consent. It says outstanding matters, including boundaries, will be resolved through dialogue. The leaders directed the foreign secretaries to work on boundary-related issues, according to The Times of India.

The document also revives a High-Level Monitoring Group, led by Nepal's Foreign Secretary and India's Ambassador to Nepal, to meet at least once every six months. The India-Nepal Joint Commission is to meet next in 2027.

The leaders agreed to make the Kathmandu–Bhairahawa–Lucknow air route two-way. BBC News reported that Nepal had sought wider access to Indian airspace for its Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports and that this was not agreed. Analyst Anil Trigunayat told the BBC the Pokhara airport "can pose certain security challenges for India".

"The bond between India and Nepal is not merely one of neighborhood, but of belonging and unshakeable trust," Modi said. Shah said the leaders held "candid, substantive, and forward-looking discussions" and invited Modi to visit Nepal.
keyFacts: The package is worth ₹15,000 crore (NPR 24,000 crore): ₹3,500 crore in grants, ₹11,500 crore line of credit.

The next India-Nepal Joint Commission meeting is set for 2027.
stories.background: Shah, 36, a former rapper and Kathmandu mayor, became prime minister after his Rastriya Swatantra Party won 182 of 275 seats in the March 5 election. That vote followed protests in September 2025 that led KP Sharma Oli to resign. A flash flood and mudslide in Rasuwa district on August 26 killed at least 675 people, Scroll reported. The two countries have an unresolved boundary dispute.
stories.whyItMatters: The package funds Nepal's flood reconstruction and energy projects, and the port access eases the transit trade of a landlocked country that depends heavily on India.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks in Antalya end without agreement after dispute over fossil fuels
stories.dek: About 130 countries demanded explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels, while Saudi Arabia, Russia and other producers opposed any reference; climate finance was a second point of division.
stories.summary: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday without an agreed final text after countries rejected the proposed Antalya Pact. The split was over whether to name fossil fuels, and over money for developing nations.
body: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday without an agreement after countries rejected the proposed Antalya Pact two days past the talks' official deadline, according to the New York Times and DW.

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and president of COP31. The New York Times and Ars Technica reported it was the first time since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 that the talks closed without a consensus deal.

The main dispute was over the words "fossil fuels". DW and the BBC reported that about 130 parties, including island nations, developing countries and EU members, called for the phrase to be reinserted. The BBC said that is roughly two-thirds of the countries in Antalya. The call failed, and many refused to back the text.

A group of oil producers led by Saudi Arabia, and including Russia, had blocked any mention of fossil fuels, the New York Times reported. Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking for the 22 Arab League countries, said Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical emissions and had a right to choose their own approach. Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko said: "For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel."

EU representative Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's minister, called a deal without a mention of fossil fuels "unconscionable", the BBC reported. Kurum had urged governments not to get "hung up on one word or phrase". Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who co-led the negotiations, cited "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".

Finance was a second fault line. Developing countries want more money to move away from coal, oil and gas and to cope with warming. The BBC said the EU had ruled out significant new funding before the talks began. Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa accused Europe of refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance. Mongabay India reported that India challenged setting new global targets without addressing who had used up the carbon budget and who must pay for the transition.

The United States sent no official delegation. The BBC reported that, while talks ran in Antalya, the leaders of the US, China and Russia issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process, the BBC reported. Some governments have proposed voting when consensus fails; others want willing countries to make deals outside the formal talks. France 24 reported disappointment across Africa over the outcome.

DW reported that more than 90 countries pledged to pursue a Turkey-led electrification goal, although it was not formally adopted. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels is due in Tuvalu in July 2027.
keyFacts: COP31 in Antalya ended on Sunday without adopting the proposed Antalya Pact.
About 130 parties sought explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels.
It was the first collapse of a final deal since COP15 in 2009.
The US sent no official delegation to Antalya.
The next Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels conference is in Tuvalu in July 2027.
stories.background: The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared in a closing COP decision at COP28 in Dubai three years ago, which promised a transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. DW reported it has been left out of every text since. UN climate decisions require consensus among all countries.
stories.whyItMatters: Without an agreed text, the summit produced no shared political direction on emissions or on money for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Reform of the consensus-based process is now under discussion.

stories.headline: Iran says three ships caught fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
stories.dek: The Revolutionary Guards' claim came as the US Treasury sanctioned Iran-linked networks and Qatar's prime minister met Vance and Rubio in Washington.
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. On Monday the US sanctioned 22 entities and eight people tied to Iran, while Qatar's prime minister pressed Washington to revive talks.
body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Al Jazeera's reporting. The claim has not been independently confirmed in the material reviewed, and no details on the ships or any casualties were given.
Iranian forces have announced several incidents in recent weeks of ships catching fire while using routes Tehran considers off-limits, The Hindu reported.

Separately, Iran's military said it shot down a US "Lockheed drone" over the Persian Gulf, east of the strait, The Indian Express reported. That is Iran's account; no US response was included in the sources.

On Monday, November 23, the US Treasury sanctioned 22 entities and eight individuals linked to Iran, in finance, oil, industry and trade. Fox News reported that the Office of Foreign Assets Control targeted exchange houses and front companies in Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey, accused of moving billions of dollars for Tehran.

Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network had identified about $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking. Foreign banks that knowingly facilitate significant transactions for the sanctioned networks risk losing access to US correspondent accounts.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement: "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baqaei, said Tehran would "use all available means to counter U.S. aggression". He described the sanctions and the naval blockade as military aggression and cited Article 51 of the UN Charter. He said the strait could be restored to security quickly if Washington met its commitments, including lifting the blockade.

In Washington, Qatar's Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, met Secretary of State Marco Rubio for a US-Qatar Strategic Dialogue. He also met Vice President J.D. Vance at the White House, according to a person familiar with the meeting who was not named. The Indian Express quoted him as saying the region could not withstand another round of tension.
The State Department said Rubio expressed appreciation for Qatar's mediation efforts. The joint statement announced no new policy direction.

President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday he was inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if there is no deal. The Hindu reported he had said at a Friday news conference that he wanted "a real deal, not a fake deal."
keyFacts: US Treasury sanctioned 22 entities and eight individuals tied to Iran on November 23.

stories.background: War broke out on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran has sought to block the Strait of Hormuz, and the US responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and sanctions. Diplomacy has stalled since a June deal collapsed. Mediators have proposed easing Hormuz disruptions in exchange for limited sanctions relief.
stories.whyItMatters: The Strait of Hormuz is vital to global energy supplies, and shipping incidents there affect oil trade. Stalled talks leave open the possibility of renewed US strikes, which allies in the region fear.

perspectives.summary: Washington says the sanctions aim to dismantle Iran's shadow banking network, and Trump says he wants a real deal and may resume strikes after the new year if none emerges.

stories.headline: Ukraine says sea drones sank Russian corvette Merkury at Libyan port
stories.dek: Libya's eastern government asked the UN to investigate whether the attack was launched from the west, while Libyan officials said the ship was badly damaged, not sunk.
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit a cargo ship off Benghazi on Sunday. Libya's eastern government has asked the UN to investigate, and two Libyan officials said the warship was severely damaged.
body: Ukraine said it sank the Russian corvette Merkury with sea drones at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, and hit a Russian cargo ship, the MV Angara, in the same operation, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy said on X on Monday that seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used and that a Ka-27 helicopter on the corvette was also destroyed. He called it "an exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war" and said the targets had been achieved. He said the Merkury was commissioned in 2023.

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said the drones were taken to a designated location and launched from a "mother ship" near the target. It said the Angara was sanctioned and carried Russian military equipment, and that the Merkury had escorted it. Russian defences tried to intercept the drones, the SBU said.

Accounts from Libya differ on the outcome. Two Libyan officials told The Associated Press the corvette was severely damaged, not sunk. They said at least four drones were intercepted and two hit the ship, and that at least 10 people, Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded. The officials are affiliated with the Libyan National Army and spoke anonymously. Ambrey, a UK-based maritime security firm, said some explosions were probably caused by ammunition detonating aboard the Merkury.
Libya's coast guard said another sea drone struck a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel off Benghazi hours later. The sources do not say whether that vessel is the Angara.

Osama Hamad, prime minister of the eastern-based government, said he had asked the United Nations to investigate "suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya" and to verify whether Ukrainian military experts operate there. The eastern government sent a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the Security Council. The Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, which governs the west, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Libyan officials told AP earlier this year that Ukrainian forces, mostly drone experts, work in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West. They said the forces were based mainly at an air base in Misrata, with a presence in Tripoli and Zawiya.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the attack. He said Russia's Defence Ministry would give more information "if deemed to be appropriate".

Morgan Murphy, a former US defence department press secretary, told Fox News Digital the strike was "a serious escalation" that could strain ties between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump. Mykola Bielieskov of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv told Reuters that Ukraine is seeking leverage through "horizontal escalation".
The attack came as US-backed peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv resumed this month after a nine-month pause.
keyFacts: Zelenskyy said seven naval drones were used in the Sunday attack on the Merkury at Benghazi.
Two Libyan officials said the corvette was severely damaged, not sunk; at least 10 people were wounded.
Libya's eastern government wrote to the UN seeking an investigation into possible launches from western Libya.
The site is about 2,400 kilometres from the front line in Ukraine, according to The Hindu.
Peskov declined to comment; Russia's Defence Ministry may give details later.
stories.background:
Benghazi lies in eastern Libya, controlled by commander Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army, which has ties with Russia. The Institute for the Study of War reported that the Merkury stopped there for several days under a cooperation agreement to refuel and resupply while escorting cargo vessels.

In March, Russia's Transport Ministry alleged Ukrainian naval drones launched from Libya attacked the LNG carrier Arctic Metagaz; Kyiv never claimed that attack. On Saturday, a drone strike set fire to the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, and Finland's military said Ukraine likely carried it out.
stories.whyItMatters: The strike extends the war to the Mediterranean and puts Libya's divided authorities in the dispute. It also comes during resumed peace talks.

stories.headline: Supreme Court tells Bengal SIR tribunals to hear deleted voters' appeals first
stories.dek: The bench also ordered more tribunals and asked the West Bengal government to respond to claims that deleted voters are being denied ration and welfare benefits.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday directed West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals to hear appeals by voters removed from the rolls ahead of other cases, and ordered more tribunals. Appeals from Kolkata Municipal Corporation wards are to be heard first, with civic polls expected.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing West Bengal's special intensive revision (SIR) appeals to give priority to voters whose names were deleted from the electoral rolls, and ordered an increase in the number of tribunals.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana told the tribunals to separate appeals into two categories: those by voters challenging their deletion, and those challenging the inclusion of other electors. Scroll, citing Bar and Bench, reported that the court said appeals seeking exclusion of names could be deferred because they "do not involve any urgency".

The Times of India reported that 22 lakh of the 38 lakh pending appeals were filed by deleted voters. Scroll put the total at 38.3 lakh. It said the Election Commission had earlier told the court that at least 16.1 lakh appeals challenged the inclusion of voters.

Among the deleted voters' appeals, those from wards of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) are to be heard first because civic elections are approaching. Scroll, citing The Hindu, reported that these appeals must be heard within a week. It said municipal elections are expected before December 7.

The court asked the Calcutta High Court chief justice, in consultation with the Election Commission, to increase the number of tribunals, currently 19. It also asked the Commission to requisition more space for them, and Scroll reported that it suggested premises in central Kolkata or near the airport.

Advocate Prashant Bhushan told the court that more than 90% of the 1.4 lakh appeals decided so far had been allowed, restoring names to the rolls, according to The Times of India. Scroll reported his figures as about one lakh appeals disposed of and 93% of appellants found eligible. He argued that the sample supported letting appellants vote in coming elections.

Bhushan, backed by senior advocate G Sankaranarayanan, also alleged that the state government is denying deleted voters ration through the public distribution system and benefits under welfare schemes including Annapurna Yojna. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta called the claims "bald assertions" and said petitioners had not cited a single example. The bench asked the state government to file a response.

Separately, the court postponed to Wednesday the state's appeal against a Calcutta High Court division bench order barring the state election commission from announcing a KMC poll schedule. The state increased the wards from 144 to 209 through an amending Act. Mehta said the High Court wrongly concluded that the state lacked jurisdiction to do so.
keyFacts: The bench comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
Of about 38 lakh appeals, 22 lakh were filed by deleted voters, per The Times of India.
West Bengal currently has 19 appellate tribunals.
The state's appeal over the KMC ward increase from 144 to 209 will be heard Wednesday.
stories.background: The SIR in West Bengal was carried out before the April Assembly elections. Scroll reported that about 91 lakh voters, nearly 11.9% of the electorate before the revision, had been removed by April 6. The tribunals, made up of former High Court chief justices and judges, were set up after a Supreme Court order on March 10 and began hearing appeals in April. In September, the Election Commission told the court it was considering raising the number to 42. In May, the court upheld the legality of the revision but said the Commission cannot decide whether a person is an Indian citizen.
stories.whyItMatters: Voters excluded from the rolls, especially in Kolkata wards, may get their appeals decided before the civic elections. The court's order on welfare benefits could affect deleted voters who say they are being denied ration.

perspectives.label: Petitioners
perspectives.summary: Bhushan argued that the high rate of appeals allowed shows wrongful deletions, justifying priority hearings, and that deleted voters are being denied ration and welfare benefits.

perspectives.label: State government
perspectives.summary: Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the welfare allegations were bald assertions with no single example cited, and defended the state's authority to increase KMC wards.

stories.headline: Lawmakers from both parties press Nvidia on Huang's return; Senate hearing set for Dec 3
stories.dek: Republican and Democratic members of Congress said the board's reinstatement of Jensen Huang does not end questions over alleged chip smuggling to China.
stories.summary: US lawmakers from both parties criticised Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and demanded answers on alleged chip diversion to China. Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
body: US lawmakers from both parties criticised Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, saying Congress still has questions about alleged smuggling of advanced AI chips to China, and Huang is due before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.

Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, a Republican, said the hearing would be public, according to CNA. TechCrunch cited a notice on the committee's website. Huang's personal spokesperson declined to comment on the planned appearance.

Huang resigned earlier this month after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. The New York Times reported that US intelligence identified her as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board reversed course on Sunday.

President Donald Trump told CNBC he had pressed the board to bring Huang back and did not think it would have done so without his action. In a statement he wrote that the government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security", and that the Attorney General had confirmed it holds no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who chairs the Intelligence Committee, said the dispute over Nvidia and Megaspeed was "just the tip of the iceberg" and was not resolved by Huang's return. He called for passage of his Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to track advanced processors and notify the government if they suspect the chips have reached prohibited users.

The Republican chairs of three House committees, John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast, said Huang and Nvidia's Tim Teter had confirmed transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2. Republican Senator John Curtis said the board had said the previous week it did not intend to reinstate Huang. "I'd like to know what changed," he said. Republican Senator John Kennedy said he expected Huang to invoke the Fifth Amendment, "but we'll give him a chance to explain."

Democrats also pressed for action. Senator Elizabeth Warren, due to chair the Banking Committee from January, called the decision "reckless". Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said it showed the need to toughen export limits, and incoming House speaker Hakeem Jeffries said the annual defence bill should include "ironclad" provisions to keep AI technology from China.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio left a State Department press event without answering when reporters asked whether Huang's reinstatement was a national security risk, Fox News reported. The Washington Post and The New York Times, as cited by Fox, reported that Rubio had earlier warned officials about Huang's relationship. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has criticised what he called a "culture of noncompliance" at the company.
The US commerce department also added Singapore-based Megaspeed and its subsidiaries in Thailand and Malaysia to a trade blacklist on Monday, according to The Guardian.
keyFacts: Huang is scheduled to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
House panels have transcribed interviews with Huang and Tim Teter on December 1 and 2.
The commerce department added Megaspeed and its Thai and Malaysian units to a trade blacklist on Monday.
Trump told CNBC he pressed Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang.
stories.background: Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO earlier this month after reports of extramarital relationships, one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. The New York Times reported that US intelligence identified her as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Singapore's prime minister said, per The Guardian, that it investigated her but found no basis for prosecution.

stories.headline: US adds Megaspeed and six other firms to export blacklist after Huang's return to Nvidia
stories.dek: The Commerce Department's entity list notice bars the Singapore-based data centre company from US exports without a licence that is likely to be refused.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department on Monday added Singapore-based Megaspeed, its subsidiaries and other entities to its entity list over concerns about diverting advanced AI chips. The notice followed Nvidia's reinstatement of chief executive Jensen Huang, whose relationship with a former Megaspeed executive prompted scrutiny.
body: The US Commerce Department on Monday added Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian companies to its entity list, a trade blacklist, citing a risk that they divert advanced computing products to unauthorised users, according to a Federal Register filing.

The notice came hours after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive. Megaspeed is a cloud computing and data centre operator, and Nvidia, the maker of the chips widely used to run AI systems, is among its suppliers.

The restrictions cover all items subject to US Export Administration Regulations. Licence applications will be reviewed under a "presumption of denial", meaning approval is unlikely. The filing cited a "significant risk" of diversion of advanced computing products.

The listed entities include Megaspeed's units in Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia, among them Speedmatrix, MSFusion and PT Megaspeed International. The filing identified 7Road International as an alias used by the Singapore and Thailand entities. Commerce also added Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore subsidiary of Alibaba, according to Reuters. Alibaba said it would pursue all legal avenues and that Apex had never diverted restricted chips.

Commerce and the Justice Department said in a joint statement that the investigation began in 2024 after the department spotted suspicious activity. In May 2025 investigators asked Nvidia for records of sales to Megaspeed, and Nvidia put the company on its "no sell" list the next month. US and Singaporean officials also carried out an on-site check in June 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang, then Megaspeed's chief executive. The Justice Department later took the lead in a criminal inquiry.

Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, is reported to have had a relationship with him. US officials suspected her of links to Chinese intelligence, and China has called the accusations "groundless". Megaspeed said last week that it operates lawfully and that she left the company in August 2025.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this month that Treasury, the Pentagon, the State Department and the US trade representative's office had wanted Megaspeed listed for months, adding that "Commerce holds the pen". Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Commerce still needed to explain to Congress why the action took so long.

The Indian Express, citing a New York Times report, said the listing may have limited practical effect because it does not cover shipments from other countries, and most advanced chips are made in Taiwan. Critics quoted in that report called it possibly more symbolic than effective.

Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said investigations into Megaspeed were continuing. "We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America's export controls," he said. Huang and Nvidia's chief legal officer are next due to give a closed-door briefing to the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

stories.headline: Asian stocks jump as Nvidia's Huang returns; Taiwan's index gains 9.1%
stories.dek: Nvidia shares rose 31.5% on Wall Street on Monday, lifting chip-linked stocks across Asia, while Indian equity markets stayed closed for Guru Nanak Jayanti.
stories.summary: Asian shares rallied on Tuesday after Nvidia surged 31.5% on Wall Street following Jensen Huang's return as chief executive. Taiwan's benchmark rose 9.1%, the Kospi 7.5% and Japan's Nikkei 4.5%.
body: Asian shares rose sharply on Tuesday after Nvidia's 31.5% jump on Wall Street, with Taiwan's benchmark gaining 9.1%, South Korea's Kospi 7.5% and Japan's Nikkei 4.5%, as Jensen Huang returned as the chipmaker's chief executive.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan climbed 4.6%, recovering from an eight-month low and heading for its biggest single-day gain in two weeks. The Nikkei rose as traders returned from a local holiday.

Nvidia's Monday gain was its biggest one-day percentage rise in 23 years and restored nearly $1 trillion in market value, according to Reuters. CNBC reported that the shares had lost nearly 33% from November 8, when Huang admitted to an extramarital affair, before his reinstatement by the board.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq Composite 6.5%. The Nasdaq 100 rose more than 6%. S&P 500 futures were flat early on Tuesday, and Nasdaq futures slipped 0.2%.

Nvidia's partners and suppliers led the gains in Asia. CNBC reported that TSMC rose almost 10%, as did Hon Hai Precision Industry, also known as Foxconn, and Mediatek. Taipei's exchange has a daily price limit of 10% for stocks.

In South Korea, Samsung Electronics gained 8% and SK Hynix 10%. CNBC said the two make up over 40% of the Kospi's weighting. The index's rise triggered a sidecar curb on programme trading on the Korea Exchange. The South China Morning Post reported the Kospi at 5,047.15 in morning trade.
In Japan, SoftBank Group climbed over 8%, Advantest 15% and Tokyo Electron 12%, CNBC reported.

"Jensen's return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia's leadership crisis," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said in a note. She said the recovery would likely favour established companies with visible orders, strong balance sheets and pricing power.

Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, told Reuters the return had eased fear and uncertainty about the AI trade "at least at the margins". He said concerns about slowing AI investment and moderating earnings growth remained, along with uncertainty over US interest rates.

The rebound also revived bets on Federal Reserve tightening. CME Group's FedWatch tool showed traders pricing a December rate rise as a certainty, against 89% odds on Friday. The 10-year Treasury yield was at 4.94%, and the dollar stood near a more than 19-month high against the euro.
Brent crude was flat at $89.50 a barrel after falling 3.5% on Monday. Spot gold rose 0.7% to $3,657.97 an ounce.

India's NSE and BSE were shut on Tuesday for Guru Nanak Jayanti. On Monday the Sensex fell 1,483.72 points, or 1.77%, to 82,435.99, and the Nifty lost 450.95 points to 25,349.65. Trading resumes on the next business day, and investors await Wednesday's US PCE price index data.

stories.headline: NATO's Rutte vows to defend against space threats after Russian satellite report
stories.dek: German broadcasters cite Western intelligence saying Russia could launch a nuclear-capable satellite within about 60 days; the Kremlin calls the claims unsubstantiated.
stories.summary: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space, after German media reported Russia may soon launch a nuclear-capable satellite. The Kremlin dismissed the reports, while Poland and Finland reported separate Russian airspace incidents.
body: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in Berlin on Monday that the alliance would defend against threats in space, responding to German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-capable satellite.

The reports, published on November 23 by broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, cite Western intelligence agencies. They say Russia has assembled a satellite called "Sputnik-S", reportedly stored in the Moscow region for several years. France 24 said the reports also cited unnamed German military and BND spy agency sources.

According to Fox News, which summarised the German investigation, intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November said the satellite could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible. Senior officials, including Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, were reportedly briefed.

Rutte said: "I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," according to Reuters. He said NATO's defence planning covers space and that the alliance has response options it cannot always disclose. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside him, called the allegations "shocking" but said concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new.

The Kremlin rejected the reports. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said: "We haven't seen the report. But there are so many 'alleged' and 'possible' claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it's certainly hardly worth taking them seriously." Russia's embassy in Berlin called the reporting propaganda and said Moscow's space activities are peaceful and consistent with international obligations.

Fox News noted that it remains unclear whether the satellite already carries a warhead and whether Western agencies have independently verified the launch preparations. It said it had asked the White House, Pentagon, US Space Command and the German embassy for comment.

Separately, NPR reported that three Russian cruise missiles struck a rural part of south-eastern Poland, about 30 miles from the Ukrainian border, on Friday. No one was hurt. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it an "intentional provocation". Rutte said Polish authorities should complete their investigation into whether it was intentional. Reuters reported that Polish armed forces said a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle briefly violated Polish airspace.

In Finland, the foreign ministry said on Monday it had summoned Russia's ambassador after a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace on Saturday. The helicopter incident came hours after a Ukrainian drone hit the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Finland called Russia's actions in Europe "dangerous and reckless".
Merz said European leaders would discuss strengthening defence on NATO's eastern flank at an EU summit later this week.
keyFacts: German outlets reported on November 23 that Russia may launch a nuclear-capable satellite within about 60 days.
The Kremlin said the report's claims were "hardly worth taking seriously".
Three Russian cruise missiles landed in south-eastern Poland on Friday; no one was hurt.

An EU summit later this week is to discuss defence on NATO's eastern flank.
stories.background: The US Defense Intelligence Agency said in its 2026 space security assessment, published in October, that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. Fox News reported that placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.
stories.whyItMatters: Satellites support navigation, communications, financial transactions and weather forecasting, and Fox News cited the DIA as saying a nuclear detonation in orbit could disable thousands of them.

stories.headline: No dates yet for Winter Session as Monsoon Session stays unprorogued over 100 days
stories.dek: Congress has criticised the government over the delay; The Hindu reports the Winter Session has been skipped only four times, each in exceptional circumstances.
stories.summary: No dates have been announced for Parliament's Winter Session, and the Monsoon Session has still not been prorogued more than 100 days on. Congress has attacked the government, while speculation grows of a short special session on a delimitation Bill.
body: No dates have been announced for the Winter Session of Parliament, and the Monsoon Session has not been prorogued more than 100 days after it ended, according to reports by NDTV, The Hindu and The Times of India published on Monday.

The Hindu reported that Parliament has now remained unprorogued for longer than 100 days, a record. Prorogation is the formal end of a session. Until it happens, the Monsoon Session technically continues.

The Times of India reported that Congress criticised the government over the situation. The full text of its report and of NDTV's was not available, so the specific charges and any government response could not be confirmed.

The Hindu said speculation has grown that the government may convene a short special session to consider the delimitation Bill. The report did not say who was behind the speculation, and no official announcement was cited.

The Hindu also reported that the Winter Session has been skipped only four times in India's parliamentary history. It said each instance was linked to exceptional circumstances: the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
The reports did not carry a statement from the government on when the Winter Session would be held.

stories.headline: CJP's Saurav Das says he was stopped at Delhi airport from flying to Oxford
stories.dek: The Cockroach Janta Party leader says immigration staff told him his passport had been flagged; a Delhi Police official told Hindustan Times the force was unaware of the matter.
stories.summary: Cockroach Janta Party leader Saurav Das said on Monday he was stopped at Delhi airport's immigration counter and barred from a London flight to speak at Oxford. The government had not responded, and a Delhi Police official said immigration officials were involved.
body: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Saurav Das said on Monday that he was stopped at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport and prevented from boarding a flight to London, where he was due to speak at the University of Oxford.

Das said he reached the immigration counter before a flight scheduled for 1 am and was told his passport had been flagged. In a video on Instagram, he said: "I was informed that my passport has been flagged by the coward government to stop me from going out of the country."

He wrote on X: "I have been stopped by this cowardly Modi Govt at the Delhi Airport from flying to London to deliver a lecture at the University of Oxford." He said he had been invited by Oxford, Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Edinburgh to speak on what he called the cockroach movement, at events organised by Indian students.
Accounts of the host differ slightly. Das told one outlet the Oxford University Students' Union had invited him for a panel discussion. The CJP said he had been invited to address the Oxford Union.
Das said the incident would not deter him and that he would travel to London, Paris and other places in future.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke backed him on X. "Saurav was invited to speak at a conference at the University of Oxford, but looks like some anpadh gawar in power, who himself loves travelling around the world, is jealous of Saurav getting an invitation from Oxford," Dipke wrote. The CJP said the government feared educated voices.

The government had not responded to the allegations, News18 reported. A Delhi Police official told Hindustan Times that police were not aware of the matter and that immigration officials were involved. None of the reports said who flagged the passport or on what grounds.

Das and CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka were held in Tihar jail after entering Jantar Mantar, which had been de-notified as a protest site, and waving the national flag on October 13. They were released on October 21 on personal and surety bonds of ₹50,000 each.

stories.headline: SP and Congress hold first seat-sharing talks for 2027 Uttar Pradesh polls
stories.dek: Congress shared a list of about 130 preferred seats in a meeting of around 20 minutes; the two sides are likely to meet again on Tuesday.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party and Congress held their first round of seat-sharing talks in New Delhi on Monday for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav said the alliance would be finalised soon.
body: The Samajwadi Party (SP) and Congress held the first round of seat-sharing talks for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections in New Delhi on Monday, with leaders from both sides saying an alliance deal could be finalised soon.

The meeting took place at the residence of Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pramod Tiwari. The Hindu reported that it lasted about 20 minutes, while the New Indian Express put the duration at 15 minutes. The New Indian Express headline said a final agreement was expected in three days. The Hindu reported that the two sides were likely to meet again on Tuesday.

Ram Gopal Yadav, the SP national general secretary and Rajya Sabha MP who led his party's team, described the atmosphere as cordial. "We listened to each other's points of view, and we will soon finalise this alliance and inform you about it," he told reporters.

Rajendra Pal Gautam, the Uttar Pradesh Congress in-charge, said both parties trust each other and will manage matters jointly. The Hindu cited sources as saying this was only a first round and that agreement on the state's 403 Assembly seats would take time.

A Congress leader who took part, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the party had shared a list of around 130 preferred seats. He said the demand rested on the 2024 Lok Sabha results and the party's record in earlier Assembly elections. "In the assembly segments coming under six Lok Sabha seats we won in 2024, we are very strong," he said.

SP spokesperson Sunil Singh Yadav 'Sajan' said winnability would be the sole criterion for deciding which party contests a seat. He said SP leader Akhilesh Yadav and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had a broader understanding on defeating the BJP.

SP Lok Sabha MP Rajeev Rai told The Hindu on November 22 that his party did not want to repeat "the Bihar story". He said the alliance partner would have to show for each seat how it could win, who its likely candidate was and how that candidate fitted the constituency.

The SP team also included Lok Sabha MPs Rajeev Rai and Iqra Choudhary and state president Shyam Lal Pal. The Congress side included state president Aradhana Misra, working president Imran Masood and MLA Virendra Chaudhary. Congress held a separate meeting in the evening to review the SP's response.

stories.headline: Madurai bans large gatherings as court permits Deepam at Thiruparankundram hill
stories.dek: A Tamil Nadu government report, published after a state review, says the pillar near the dargah is a British-era survey marker, not the lamp pillar.
stories.summary: Madurai's district magistrate imposed prohibitory orders from 9 pm on November 23 to 10 am on November 25, before the Karthigai Deepam festival. The Supreme Court had allowed a one-time lamp lighting on a hilltop pillar, which a state report calls a survey pillar.
body: Madurai's District Collector and District Magistrate, Nishant Krishna, imposed prohibitory orders across the district from 9 pm on Monday, November 23, ahead of the Karthigai Deepam festival on November 24 and the Supreme Court-permitted lamp lighting on Thirupparankundram hill.

The order, issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, runs until 10 am on November 25 unless withdrawn earlier. Section 163 replaces the former Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as News18 noted.

According to NDTV, the order cites reports from the Madurai City Police Commissioner, the District Superintendent of Police and the Revenue Divisional Officer of Thirumangalam. They flagged mobilisation by organisations both for and against lighting the lamp on the hilltop pillar, which stands close to the Sikandar Badusha Dargah. The administration said people from both communities, including from other districts, could gather in large numbers.

The order bans assemblies, agitations, demonstrations, processions and public meetings in the district. It also bars people from climbing the hill. Exemptions cover gatherings authorised by competent authorities, weddings, funerals and specified domestic occasions, and religious ceremonies by authorised personnel of the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple. Measures to implement the Supreme Court's November 20 order are also exempt, as are existing religious observances and access to the dargah, subject to police regulation.

On November 20, the Supreme Court allowed a team authorised by the temple administration to light the lamp on the pillar, which petitioners identify as the Deepathoon, on November 24 as a one-time measure with security safeguards. The court said this creates no permanent customary, religious or proprietary right over the site and does not displace existing observances near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple.
The Tamil Nadu government has filed a review petition seeking reconsideration and a stay. NDTV reported that it was not listed for hearing on Monday.

Separately, The Hindu reported on a 2026 report by the state's Departments of Survey and Settlement and Archaeology. It says the pillar near the dargah is a Great Trigonometrical Survey pillar erected by the British, and that the original Deepathoon lies below the dargah. The report says triangulation bearings from the hill match values in the colonial-era survey.

Politically, M K Stalin has questioned the government's handling of the case, and the BJP has criticised the state for challenging the order. The VCK has voiced reservations about implementing it, and the Left parties have raised concern about longstanding religious arrangements. Congress and the IUML have said they will back the government's decision. Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has not made an unequivocal public statement, NDTV reported.
The prohibitory orders remain in force until 10 am on November 25.

The Supreme Court's November 20 order allows a one-time lamp lighting on November 24.
The state's report spans five volumes and over 1,800 pages.
The Revenue Department allowed publication of the report in August 2026.

Petitioners say a stone pillar atop the hill is the Deepathoon, while customary observances take place near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple. The state ordered a survey of Great Trigonometrical Survey stations in December 2025.

stories.headline: India and China end second round of corps commander talks on Arunachal frontier
stories.dek: The discussions, which ran for nearly 10 days with a short break, focused on protocols to prevent face-offs between troops before winter sets in.
stories.summary: India and China concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks on easing friction along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh, Ministry of Defence sources said. The talks began on November 8 and ran for nearly 10 days.
body: India and China have concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks on reducing friction along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh, sources in the Ministry of Defence said.
The closely guarded discussions began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, and continued for nearly 10 days with a short break. The sources described the talks as cordial.

Lieutenant-General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army's III Corps, led the Indian delegation. The corps, also known as the Spear Corps, is headquartered at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland. His Chinese counterpart and other military officers took part, and an official from the Ministry of External Affairs was also present.

The talks focused on engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops, keeping communication channels open and reducing tensions in the eastern sector. Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.

The Hindu reported that it is unclear whether the measures discussed will be put into effect on the ground before winter sets in fully. Winter conditions along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh can be severe, affecting troop sustenance, movement and logistics, and access to forward areas becomes harder as temperatures fall.

The first round was held on September 6 and 7, 2026, at the Wacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting point in the Kibithoo sector. Wacha is India's easternmost such point. That meeting followed reports that troops of the two sides had come face to face in the Taksing area of Upper Subansiri district.

In August 2026, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the Special Representatives for boundary negotiations, held talks in Beijing. In October, Indo-Tibetan Border Police Director-General Shatrujeet Kapur, days before his retirement, said Indian and Chinese troops had faced off at multiple locations in Arunachal Pradesh.

stories.headline: UN chief Guterres urges nations to agree AI risk framework within a year
stories.dek: Speaking at a summit in Barbados, the Secretary-General said countries could start with shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight.
stories.summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday urged member states to develop a global, principles-based framework for managing AI risks within the next year. He spoke at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety in Barbados.
body: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Monday called on member states to develop, within the next year, a global framework for managing the risks of artificial intelligence, speaking at a summit on AI safety in Barbados.

"Today I call for member states to coordinate efforts and to develop within the next year a globally inclusive and principles-based multilateral framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight," he said at the Bridgetown Special Summit On AI Safety.

Guterres said a starting point could be for countries to agree on shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight, according to France 24, which reported with AFP.

He said he would advise his successor, who is due to take office in the New Year but has not yet been selected, that properly controlling AI is necessary for "humanity to maintain control of our world". Al Jazeera noted that Guterres has become more vocal on AI as the end of his term nears.

Responding to a question from AFP, Guterres said global institutions "correspond to the reality of the world in 1945". "It's clear that institutions need to be reformed in order to adapt themselves to the realities of today's world," he said. He said that applied to the UN, the international financial architecture and the world trade system.

France 24 described international regulation of AI as unlikely in the near term, because the United States and China are competing for the lead in research and development. It said US regulators, in the country where AI development is moving fastest, are unlikely to intervene.

In September, US President Donald Trump hosted a group of American technology executives who agreed to follow a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety, France 24 reported. In the same month, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk called for a slowdown in AI development, while Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Meta's Mark Zuckerberg favour moving ahead at full speed, the outlet said.

A third outlet, CXOToday, reported in a headline that OpenAI's chief scientist is seeking global limits on AI development and that Altman agrees. The full text was not available, and details of the proposal could not be confirmed.
keyFacts: Guterres spoke on Monday at the Bridgetown Special Summit On AI Safety in Barbados.
He asked member states to agree a framework within the next year.
He suggested shared safety measures, a testing regime and independent oversight requirements.
His successor is due to take office in the New Year but has not been selected.
stories.background: The UN chief's term is nearing its end. France 24 said nations recently agreed to talks on regulating autonomous weapons, which it called "killer robots", by 2028. In September, some AI company leaders urged caution at the UN, while others opposed slowing down.
stories.whyItMatters: Any shared AI safety rules would affect governments and developers worldwide, but France 24 reports that rivalry between the US and China makes binding international regulation unlikely soon.

stories.headline: 14 countries acknowledge ICJ genocide ruling on Rohingya; UK sanctions five Myanmar officers
stories.dek: Britain also said it formally recognises genocide against the Rohingya and plans legislation to stop aviation fuel supplies to Myanmar.
stories.summary: The UK and 13 other countries said on Monday they acknowledge the International Court of Justice's ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. London announced asset freezes and travel bans on five senior military figures.
body: The United Kingdom and 13 other countries said on Monday they "acknowledged" the International Court of Justice ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, as London announced sanctions on five senior military figures.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia and the UK issued a joint statement. It said Myanmar had "violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention". It added that the judgment is binding and called on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law.

The UK separately said it "formally recognises" genocide against the Rohingya. The sanctions, which include asset freezes and travel bans, target Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo, according to BBC News.

"The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said. He said Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, whom the UK sanctioned in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" because he headed the military in 2017.

The Foreign Office said Britain intends to bring in legislation on the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar. It also announced £5m in new funding for services to about 350,000 people in Rakhine state, and a further £3 million for accountability and justice for survivors of abuses across Myanmar.

Miliband called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through", a stop to air strikes on civilians and the release of political prisoners. He told MPs on Monday that air strikes and violence involving the Arakan Army were still occurring.
He said the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, with a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.

The ICJ delivered its verdict on November 19 by nine votes to six. It found that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence". The court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 operation in Rakhine. Myanmar denied the claims and its government called the ruling unfair and a "great disappointment".
Britain expelled Myanmar's defence attaché last week after the verdict.
keyFacts: Fourteen states, including the UK, issued a joint statement on Monday acknowledging the ICJ ruling.
The UK sanctioned five senior Myanmar military figures with asset freezes and travel bans.
The ICJ ruled 9–6 on November 19 that Myanmar committed genocide.
The UK is providing £5m in humanitarian funding and £3 million for accountability.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and are supported by Bangladesh.
stories.background: The ICJ ruling concerns the 2017 military operation in Rakhine state, which borders Bangladesh. Reports said entire villages were burnt and women and girls raped. Myanmar's leader at the time, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021. The ICJ ruling was the first time in its 80-year history that it found a state committed genocide.
stories.whyItMatters: The sanctions and planned fuel legislation add financial and logistical restrictions on Myanmar's military, while the funding is aimed at about 350,000 people in Rakhine state.

stories.headline: Trump attacks Newsom over death row commutations, orders push for more federal executions
stories.dek: Speaking at the Justice Department, the president signed a memorandum directing prosecutors to seek capital punishment in more cases, while Newsom's office hit back with a video.
stories.summary: President Donald Trump used a Justice Department event on Monday to criticise California Governor Gavin Newsom's commutation of 548 death sentences. He said he would sign a directive telling the Attorney General to seek the death penalty in more cases and expedite federal executions.
body: President Donald Trump on Monday criticised California Governor Gavin Newsom's decision to commute 548 death sentences, and said he would sign a directive ordering the Justice Department to seek capital punishment in more cases and to expedite federal executions.

Trump spoke at the department in Washington alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche and relatives of murder victims. "Newsom, a terrible governor in so many other ways, came along and stole away the only closure those families might ever have," Trump said.

He said the directive would order the department to seek the death penalty "for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims." The White House later released the signed memorandum, which directs the Attorney General to pursue federal jurisdiction and capital punishment in qualifying cases, consistent with applicable law.
Blanche told the families, "We have your back." He said the department is "seeking the death penalty whenever appropriate."

Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was abducted and killed in 1996, also spoke. Robert Rhoades, who was sentenced to death in 1999 for the crime, is among those whose sentences Newsom commuted, according to the New York Post.

Marc Klaas, father of 12-year-old Polly Klaas, who was killed in 1993, told the California Post he does not usually agree with Trump but that "this is a point where we converge." He questioned why Newsom had not sought to change the law earlier in the seven-plus years since imposing a moratorium on executions in 2019.

Former state Senate Majority Leader Gloria Romero delivered more than 4,000 signatures to the California Supreme Court on Monday. She is asking the justices not to approve the mass commutation, to review each case individually and to let victims' families be heard first.

Newsom announced the commutations on November 5, converting every California death sentence to life in prison without parole. He said he had concluded "the state cannot morally kill." His office says the commutations will not take effect until the necessary legal steps are completed.

Minutes before the event began, Newsom's press office released a video responding to Trump. It accused the president of selling pardons to wealthy allies and recalled his 1989 newspaper ads calling for the death penalty in the Central Park Five case. "Every person on California's former death row will die in prison," the office said. "Not one walks out."
The South China Morning Post noted that Newsom, an outspoken critic of Trump, is considering his own bid for the White House.

His office says it will not take effect until the necessary legal steps are completed, and opponents have asked the California Supreme Court to review the cases individually.

stories.headline: IMD forecasts heavy rain for Tamil Nadu and Kerala till November 27, dense fog in North
stories.dek: Easterly waves over the Bay of Bengal and off the Kerala-Karnataka coast are behind the rain, while night temperatures fall across Central, East and Northwest India.
stories.summary: The India Meteorological Department has forecast isolated heavy rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds over Tamil Nadu, Kerala and neighbouring areas till November 27. It also warned of dense morning fog in several northern, eastern and northeastern states.
body: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast isolated heavy rainfall with thunderstorms and gusty winds over parts of South Peninsular India this week, and warned of dense morning fog across several northern, eastern and northeastern states.
In its latest bulletin, the agency attributed the southern weather to troughs in the easterlies, with active easterly waves over the Bay of Bengal and off the Kerala-Karnataka coast.

Isolated heavy rain is very likely over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal from November 23 to 27, and over Kerala and Mahe from November 24 to 27. Fairly widespread to widespread showers are expected over Tamil Nadu and Puducherry from November 24 to 26, over Kerala and Mahe from November 24 to 27, and over Lakshadweep from November 25 to 28.

Isolated thunderstorms are forecast over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Rayalaseema till November 27, with winds of 40–50 kmph gusting to 60 kmph. Kerala, Mahe, Lakshadweep and coastal Andhra Pradesh can expect winds of 30–40 kmph, gusting to 50 kmph, through November 27.
One report, from theopenpress, described the easterly waves as bringing relief to Tamil Nadu after Cyclone Akvan missed the state. The bulletin details available did not cover the cyclone.

In the north, minimum temperatures will fall gradually by 3–5°C over Central India until November 26, by 3–4°C over East India until November 27, and by 2–3°C over Northwest India until November 28, the IMD said. West and Central India are expected to stay largely dry.

Dense fog is very likely in isolated pockets of Himachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura till November 25, and over Assam and Meghalaya on November 24 and 25. East Uttar Pradesh is expected to see dense fog through November 24.
The IMD cautioned that reduced visibility could disrupt airport, highway and railway operations, and pose respiratory and eye-irritation risks.

In Delhi-NCR, skies will stay mainly clear on Tuesday, with mist or shallow fog in a few places in the morning. Mist or shallow fog is forecast through November 26, with moderate fog likely in a few pockets on November 25 and 26.
Daytime maximums in the capital are forecast at 24°C to 26°C, which is 1.6°C to 3.0°C below normal at most places. Minimums are expected near normal, at 10°C to 12°C.

stories.headline: India holds third place on Lowy Asia Power Index; BJP cites it against Rahul Gandhi
stories.dek: The Australian think tank rates Modi Asia's second-most effective regional leader, while also saying perceptions of his global leadership have diminished.
stories.summary: The Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index kept India third with 40.5 points and rated Narendra Modi the second-most effective regional leader. On Monday the BJP cited the findings to criticise Rahul Gandhi's remarks about India made abroad.
body: India retained third place on the Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index, and the BJP used the findings on Monday to criticise Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi over his comments on the economy made abroad.

The Australian think tank, which published the index on Sunday, said India's score rose by 0.5 to 40.5 points out of 100. That kept it the only country in the "major power" category. The United States, at 78.9 after a fall of 1.5 points, and China, at 73.6 after a fall of 0.1, were classed as "superpowers".

The institute said India had played "a much more influential role in Asia" despite a dip in relative economic capability and a year focused on internal challenges. The gap with China was the narrowest since the index began in 2018, though Beijing's power remained 80% higher than India's, it said.

Diplomatic influence was India's strongest measure and held steady in a year when most countries faltered. India was represented in 17 of the forums Lowy tracks, level with Indonesia and Thailand and one behind China. Its defence networks and cultural influence scores also rose, the institute said, citing BrahMos missile sales to Southeast Asia among other factors.
Its economic capability score dipped slightly, which the institute attributed to a weaker rupee against the US dollar and a change in how the International Monetary Fund measures economies.

Experts rated Modi the second-most effective regional leader, behind Chinese President Xi Jinping. The institute also said perceptions of his global leadership and strategic ambition had diminished. It linked this to India's lower diplomatic profile during the Gulf conflict, citing its muted response when a US submarine sank an Iranian naval vessel that had returned from an exercise hosted by India.

Pakistan ranked sixteenth with 15 points, a gain of 0.6. The institute said it "punched above its weight" through its role in US-Iran ceasefire talks, but added that it was unlikely to sustain the score.
BJP president Nitin Nabin said: "Rahul Gandhi's agenda is no longer to discuss the country's development but to malign the nation and cast doubts on its every achievement."

BJP MP and former Union minister Ravi Shankar Prasad cited the Lowy report along with assessments by Goldman Sachs, the IMF and the World Bank. He alleged that Gandhi presents India in a negative light on foreign soil, asked whether he had "taken a lease to defame India", and asked whether he was acting at the behest of certain forces.
The sources did not carry a response from Gandhi or the Congress.
keyFacts: India scored 40.5 points on the 2026 Asia Power Index, up 0.5, keeping third place.
The US scored 78.9 and China 73.6; both are classed as superpowers.
Modi was rated Asia's second-most effective regional leader, behind Xi Jinping.
Pakistan ranked sixteenth with 15 points, a gain of 0.6.
The BJP criticised Rahul Gandhi on Monday, citing the index.
stories.background: The Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank, has published the Asia Power Index annually since 2018. It scores countries on parameters including economic and military capabilities, resilience, future resources and cultural influence. Countries above 70 points are superpowers, and the middle power threshold this year is 15 points.
stories.whyItMatters: The index feeds a political argument over how India's standing should be described, with the ruling party using it against the Leader of the Opposition.

stories.headline: India-EU trade deal could take effect by mid-2027, says EU ambassador
stories.dek: Jean-Eric Paquet expects the agreement to be signed in December, after which the European Parliament must give its assent before it can enter into force.
stories.summary: EU Ambassador Jean-Eric Paquet said on Monday that the India-EU free trade agreement is expected to be signed in December and could take effect by mid-2027. The European Parliament must first give its assent.
body: The India-European Union free trade agreement is expected to be signed in December and could enter into force by the middle of 2027, EU Ambassador to India Jean-Eric Paquet said on Monday.

Paquet made the remarks in a video message on X. He said negotiations concluded at the India-EU summit in January, after which teams from both sides worked on finalising and technically refining the text.
The European Commission proposed the agreement's signature to the Council in September, he said. European ministers are now discussing whether to approve its signing.
"The wide expectation is that we will have agreement to sign in December. And this is where we also hope to have a high-level visit coming to Europe for that signature," Paquet said.

After signing, the European Parliament will scrutinise the agreement and must give its assent before it can take effect. Paquet said the Parliament can only accept or reject the text, so the process does not reopen negotiations.

He said the Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee had recently visited Delhi and explained how the scrutiny works. He cited the committee's chair as expecting Parliament to form its view in spring and as being optimistic about a positive outcome. Paquet stressed he was quoting the chair and not speaking for the Parliament.

According to India's Commerce Ministry, the pact is expected to benefit labour-intensive sectors including textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products, gems and jewellery, handicrafts, engineering goods and automobiles. It said tariffs on nearly USD 33 billion worth of Indian exports in such sectors would fall to zero when the agreement enters into force.

The ministry said India has secured market access for agricultural and processed food products while safeguarding sensitive sectors, including dairy, cereals and poultry. The agreement also covers services, digital trade, customs and trade facilitation, intellectual property rights and the mobility of professionals.
Bilateral trade in goods between India and the EU stood at EUR 118 billion in 2025, according to the European Commission.

stories.headline: Delhi's AQI stands at 242 on Tuesday morning, with several NCR cities worse
stories.dek: Ten of the capital's monitoring stations were in the 'very poor' band, while Panchgaon in Haryana recorded the highest city-level reading in the country.
stories.summary: Delhi's average AQI was 242 at 7 am on Tuesday, in the 'poor' category, with Panchgaon in Haryana at 310 the highest nationally. Headlines also point to a study on rural NCR exposure and a Supreme Court signal on BS-VI-only vehicles.
body: Delhi's average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 242 at 7 am on Tuesday, in the 'poor' category, compared with 248 at the same hour on Monday, according to real-time Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data cited by Business Standard. PM2.5 was the prominent pollutant.

Of 57 stations in the capital with valid readings, 46 recorded AQI above 200 and 10 recorded above 300, the 'very poor' range. Sirifort had the highest reading at 336, followed by IGNOU Maidan Garhi at 333 and North Campus, Delhi University, at 322. News18, citing the Delhi Department of Environment, gave a slightly different station count: 10 'very poor', 36 'poor' and 11 'moderate'.

The lowest readings were at IMD Lodhi Road (163), Ghoga (166), Jharoda Kalan (175) and NSIT Dwarka (178), all 'moderate'. Elsewhere, Anand Vihar recorded 207, Burari 250, Chandni Chowk 265 and IGI Airport 191, according to News18.

Several NCR cities fared worse than Delhi. Among 282 cities with valid readings in the CPCB's 7 am dataset, Panchgaon recorded the highest AQI at 310, followed by Ballabgarh at 304 and Sikar in Rajasthan at 283. Dharuhera was at 282 and Gurugram at 277. Ghaziabad and Meerut were at 214 each, and Noida and Greater Noida at 211. Palwal, at 90, was among the better-performing NCR cities.

The Air Quality Early Warning System expects Delhi's air to stay 'poor' on Tuesday and Wednesday and slip to 'very poor' on November 26, News18 reported. The India Meteorological Department expects mainly clear skies over the next four days, with mist and shallow fog on November 24.

The IITM system's source-apportionment display for November 23 put stubble burning at 0.8 per cent of Delhi's daily mean PM2.5. 'Others' accounted for 32 per cent and Delhi transport for 21.5 per cent. Jhajjar contributed 10.2 per cent and Rohtak 6.1 per cent.

Two other reports carried the same morning. Deccan Herald reported a study finding rural NCR areas are exposed to higher levels of toxic air. The Indian Express reported that the Supreme Court is in favour of allowing only BS-VI vehicles in Delhi to curb pollution. Full details of both were not available.

The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) continues to list Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan as active across Delhi-NCR. It has also asked Delhi and NCR states to prepare district-level plans for 2027 aimed at cutting air pollution by 15–20 per cent.

stories.whyItMatters: Residents across Delhi-NCR face poor to very poor air, with forecasts pointing to a further decline on November 26 and possible vehicle restrictions under court consideration.
